# My Van Almost Burned Down. Here's the Post-Mortem So You Don't Have To Learn It The Way I Did.

**A fire post-mortem from a mobile groomer in Halifax — the actual numbers, what the electrician told me, and a checklist you can run on your own van this weekend.**

*Quick note before I start: I am not an electrician. I run a dog grooming van. Everything technical in this post comes from Priya at Sackville Marine Electric, who is a licensed electrician, or from notes I took while she was standing in my van explaining things. If any of this sounds like your situation, get a pro to look at it. Don't take my word for anything.*

---

## Wednesday, October 28, around 2:15pm

I was in a client's driveway in Bedford, drying Moose. He's a Bernese Mountain Dog — roughly 130 pounds of extremely happy opinion about himself — and I had him on the high setting of my dryer, the way I do for a double coat.

At some point I smelled hot plastic.

My first thought was the dryer motor. The dryer does get warm, and the previous week I'd had a client with a very nervous terrier who wouldn't let me use the clippers near him, and I'd been running the dryer hard all afternoon. So I thought: motor's cooking, I'll turn it down.

Then I looked down.

There was smoke coming out of the bench seat. The bench seat where the batteries are.

I hit the battery switch. I got Moose out the side door — still damp, tail going, thrilled about all of it, honestly, he has no idea he was in a bad situation. I had an extinguisher and I used a bit of it, though looking back I'm not sure I needed to. The lug on the positive end was black and the cable jacket had melted back about 3cm from it.

Moose's mom brought me a coffee and sat with me on her steps while I shook.

Everyone's fine. Moose is fine. I'm fine, mostly. But my van has been out of service since, and I'm off the road for weeks, and I'm kind of losing my mind, and my rent is due the 1st. So I'm writing this properly, because if it helps one person avoid this, it's worth it.

---

## What the setup was

Since this is the part that matters, here's exactly what I had, so it all makes sense:

| | |
|---|---|
| **Inverter** | 3000W, 12V |
| **Batteries** | Two 200Ah lithium, 12V system |
| **Cable, battery to inverter** | 4 AWG |
| **Fuse** | 300A ANL, mounted ~90cm from the battery |
| **Built by** | Coastline Van Fitouts (Darren), spring 2025 |
| **Load** | Dryer on high (1800–2000W), water heater sometimes |

That's it. That's the whole build. It looked great. It looked *tidy*. Cable was dressed neatly, everything was heat-shrunk, it looked like something you'd see in a showroom.

Tidy is not the same as right.

---

## What actually went wrong

Priya found four things. I've been chewing on the first two for weeks.

### 1. The cable was way too small for the load

My dryer pulls somewhere between 1800 and 2000W. The water heater adds more on top. The inverter was rated 3000W, which sounds like a lot until you do the division.

**3000W ÷ 12V = 250 amps.**

That's the number that ruined me. 250 amps is what my inverter wants at full output. 150–200 amps is what my dryer alone pulls at 12V. And my cable was 4 AWG.

Priya's recommendation: **2/0** for a 3000W inverter at 12V.

Here's the gap, roughly:

- **4 AWG copper** is good for somewhere around **70–110 amps**, depending on how it's run, whether it's bundled with other cable, and what the insulation temperature rating is. (Free air is better than stuffed in a chase in a hot van. Neither way is it 150 amps.)
- **2/0 copper** handles roughly **230–260 amps** in a typical install, which matches a 250A inverter with some headroom.

So my dryer on high was pushing about **two to three times** what that cable was rated to carry. Every appointment, for five months.

### 2. The lug was crimped with pliers

This is the actual failure point. The cable itself was undersized, but the thing that melted was the connection — the lug on the positive battery terminal.

It was crimped with pliers. Or a hammer. Not a proper crimper. And there was heat-shrink over the top of it, which meant **I could not see the joint, and neither could anyone else.**

Priya's words were that a plier-crimped lug is a connection that may or may not be making metal-to-metal contact, and if it isn't, all of that current has to squeeze through whatever *is* touching. That contact point turns into a tiny space heater.

The math is the part I can't stop thinking about. Heat generated is current squared times resistance (I²R):

| The joint | Resistance | Heat at 250 amps |
|---|---|---|
| A proper crimp | ~0.0002 Ω | **~13 watts** |
| A plier-crimped lug | ~0.05–0.1 Ω | **3,000–6,000 watts** |

Six thousand watts in a joint the size of your thumb. That's a blowtorch. That's what melted the lug black and cooked the insulation back 3cm. Meanwhile the cable itself was also generating heat along its whole length — over a three-metre round trip at 250 amps, 4 AWG is putting out roughly 150 watts of heat on its own — so the whole run was warm and the bad joint was the hottest point in the van.

**The heat-shrink is what made this dangerous.** Without it I might have *seen* the damage. With it, everything looked finished and professional, so I trusted it.

### 3. The fuse was in the wrong place

The fuse itself — 300A ANL — is a reasonable rating for a 250A inverter. Priya isn't going to knock that choice.

But it was mounted **90cm from the battery**, and she says it should have been within about **18cm** (7 inches) of the positive terminal.

Why does that matter? Because the fuse protects the *cable*, and only the cable it sits directly on. Those first 90cm of cable between the battery and the fuse were unprotected. If that section had shorted, the 300A fuse down the line would have done nothing for it. That whole stretch needed to be as short as possible — ideally under 18cm — so there's almost no unprotected wire anywhere in the van.

And here's the other half of it: a 300A fuse on a cable rated for ~100 amps is a fuse that can never protect the cable. It protects against a dead short, not against overloading the wire. The wire was overloaded by a factor of three. The fuse would never have saved me.

Priya's recommendation was a **Class T fuse block**, which is what she uses in her marine installs. That's her call and it makes sense to me — but the lesson isn't "ANL bad, Class T good." The lesson is **fuse placement, and the fact that the fuse has to match the smallest wire in the run.**

### 4. There was no smoke detector in the back

Just the one in the cab that came with the van.

The failure happened inside the bench seat cavity. Batteries under there, cable under there, and the first sign I had was smoke *coming out of the seat*. I never saw the glow. I never smelled the insulation starting to cook — I smelled hot plastic about a second before I saw smoke, and I was lucky, because I was sitting right next to it.

If that seat had been in a different position, or if I'd been at the other end of the van, or if I'd had the dryer running on high and walked away for two minutes — that's a different story.

---

## Priya showed me something that stuck with me

She pulled up photos of my damage next to thermal camera shots of her own van running the same kind of load. Same inverter class, same kind of dryer, same battery bank.

**Hers barely gets warm.**

Same power. Completely different result. Because her cable is the right size for the current, so the current isn't fighting its way through copper that's too thin, and her connections are properly made, so there's no joint turning into a space heater. The heat has somewhere to go.

I keep thinking about that comparison. It's not that her van is a better van. It's that the numbers work out in hers and they didn't in mine.

---

## What I'm having done

**$4,200.** Rewire the main runs with properly sized cable, new fuse block, Class T fuse. Minimum three weeks — parts are on order.

**31 appointments cancelled so far.** My insurance adjuster is coming Thursday. Everyone's fine and the clients have been incredibly understanding, but my income is that van. Rent is due the 1st.

Darren hasn't answered my three texts and my email. I'm not going to sit here and diagnose his work or tell you what he did wrong — I genuinely don't know what happened in his shop, and it may have been a subcontractor, or a bad day, or something else entirely. I'm just going to tell you what happened in my van and what an independent electrician told me, and let people decide for themselves.

---

## Tasha — please read this part before you pay your deposit

Tasha, I know you're about to put money down with Darren for your build and I want to be really clear that **this is not me telling you not to.** You're the one who has to live in that van and do the work, and only you and your builder can decide.

But get the answers **in writing, before the deposit**, in an email so there's a record of it. If someone won't put the specs in writing, that's your answer.

Here's exactly what to ask. Copy this:

1. **What AWG cable are you using for the battery-to-inverter run on a 3000W/12V inverter?** Both positive and negative?
2. **What's the total run length, and how is it routed?** Bundled with other cable, or free air? Anything pinched through a body panel?
3. **What fuse type and rating, and how far from the positive battery terminal is the fuse mounted?** (Should be within about 18cm / 7 inches.)
4. **Is every battery lug crimped with a proper hydraulic or ratcheting crimper?** Is the lug copper and rated for the wire size?
5. **Is the heat-shrink going over the lug terminal, or over the cable?** (Over the lug hides the joint — that's how mine failed and nobody could see it.)
6. **Is there a separate fuse on each battery, or one fuse for the whole bank?**
7. **Is there a battery switch, and can I reach it without climbing into the cargo area?**
8. **Is there a smoke or heat detector inside the cargo area, near the battery compartment?** Is the compartment accessible for inspection and ventilated?
9. **Is there a fire blanket or thermal barrier between the battery bank and the rest of the van?**
10. **What's the inverter's continuous rating vs. peak?** What's my actual total planned load in amps at 12V?
11. **Will I get photos of the wiring before the panels and trim go on?** I'll take my own too.
12. **Do you torque the lug hardware?**
13. **Will you give me a written invoice with every part and spec listed, with your business name on it?**
14. **What's the warranty on the electrical work, in writing? Do you carry liability insurance?**
15. **Who inspects this, and will there be a signed-off inspection for my insurer?**

On #15 — talk to your insurance company *before* the work starts. Some policies ask questions about how the electrical was done. I'd rather you find that out now than after something goes wrong.

---

## Your own van: a checklist you can actually do

**Power off. Battery switch off. Keys out.** This is a "with the van cold and parked" check, not a "while you're mid-appointment" check. If you smell anything hot while you're working, that's a different list — I'll get to that.

**Find your battery bank and know where it is.**

1. **Locate the positive battery terminal.** Follow the cable from the positive post. What size is it? Is the same size used for the whole run, or does it step down somewhere?
2. **Look at the lug.** Is it real copper, or a thin alloy stamping? Is there a proper crimp, or does it look squeezed flat with visible tool marks? Is there heat-shrink over the joint? If you can't see the lug at all, that's a flag.
3. **Measure to the fuse.** If there's a fuse on the positive run, measure from the battery post to the fuse. Under about 18cm is the goal. If it's a foot and a half away, that's a conversation to have.
4. **Do the wiggle test.** With power off, gently move the cable right at the lug. If you feel a distinct click, a crackle, or movement inside the terminal, flag it. It should be solid.
5. **Look for colour.** Insulation that's browned or blackened near a terminal. A lug that's darker than the ones next to it. Heat-shrink that's bubbled, or shrunk tight and brittle-looking.
6. **Smell it.** Burnt plastic, sweet chemical smell, hot metal — especially after a long day. Get it checked before you use the van again.
7. **Check the negatives too.** Same attention. People only look at the positive.
8. **Check the routing.** Any place the cable passes through a body panel with a sharp edge? Any place it's pinched? Any zip ties cranked so tight they've cut into the jacket?
9. **Know your load.** Add up the wattage of everything you might run at once — dryer, water heater, light, vacuum, kettle if you've got one — then divide by 12. That number is your amps. Then ask whether your cable and your inverter are both rated for it.
10. **Buy an infrared thermometer.** See below.
11. **Do you have a smoke or heat detector in the cargo area?** If not, buy one. A cheap battery-powered heat detector is fine and it's the single highest-value thing on this list.
12. **Can you actually get to your batteries?** If you have to pull out a whole seat or a floor to look at them, you won't do it often enough. I know this because mine is under a bench seat and that's part of why nobody saw anything until it was already bad.
13. **Keep the compartment clear.** No towels, no chemical products, no fuel cans stored right next to the batteries.
14. **Photo everything before the panels go up.** If you're building new. Take your own photos, not just theirs.

### The $40 infrared thermometer

I bought one at Canadian Tire for **$40** and I wish I'd had it the day I bought the van.

Here's how to use it: at the end of a full appointment, with the dryer having run on high, point it at the battery lugs, at both ends of the main cable run, and at the fuse. Compare each reading to the ambient temperature.

- **Same as ambient** — good.
- **10–20°C above ambient** — write it down and pay attention. Something's not right.
- **Hot to the touch** — stop using the van and get it looked at.

I did this on Priya's van while she was there. On her setup, on the same load I was running: barely above ambient, a couple of degrees at most. On mine, before it happened, I have no idea, because I didn't have one. That's the whole point.

### Other cheap things worth doing

- A **smoke or heat detector for the cargo area**. Right now you have the cab one. The cab one does not help you at all if the fire starts behind you.
- A **fire blanket** to throw over a battery or a cable run if something goes wrong, and an **extinguisher** you can reach from the cab.
- **Ask your electrician what extinguisher to carry** based on your actual battery chemistry. Mine are lithium but I'll be honest, I couldn't tell you the chemistry off the top of my head, and Priya's making me find out — because it matters for what extinguisher to buy. (LiFePO4 isn't the same chemistry as the lithium in your phone and laptop, but I'm not going to guess in a blog post.)
- **A multimeter**, around $30–60, so you can confirm your battery switch actually kills power.
- **Gloves** you can grab in a second. A hot lug will give you a serious burn.

---

## If it happens to you

This is the list I wish I'd had on October 28th:

1. **Battery switch off first.** Before you touch a cable, before you touch the dryer, before you go looking for the source of smoke. If the switch is hard to reach, get it off anyway.
2. **Get the animals out.** Then yourself. Then the van.
3. **Don't touch the cable or the lug.** Especially not with bare hands, and not if it's blackened or melted. If it's smouldering you don't want to be the person holding the thing.
4. **Use the extinguisher if there's flame or smoke, from the cab door or the side door.** Don't crawl into the cargo area.
5. **Call 911** if there's actual flame, if the smoke is thick, or if it's not going out. A van fire is a van fire. Don't be brave about it.
6. **Do not cut or unbolt the cable while it's hot and under load.** If you can kill the switch, do that instead. (Priya's exact advice: battery off first, then deal with it.)
7. **Once it's out, don't close the doors and go home.** Leave it open, get it to a place where it can cool, and call your electrician before you touch anything again — including before you reconnect that battery.

---

## Where I'm at right now

Van's in the shop. Parts on order. Three weeks minimum, so realistically I'm looking at the second half of November, maybe longer, depending on when the cable and fuse block land. The adjuster is coming Thursday and I genuinely don't know what the insurance will do — I'd like to think that having a licensed electrician's report and photos of the damage helps.

31 appointments cancelled so far, and counting. Clients have been so kind about it that it's honestly made me tear up a bit more than I'd like to admit. Moose's mom has become a regular and she keeps texting me to check on the van.

The thing I keep coming back to isn't even the money. It's that I looked at my van and I *trusted* it, because it looked tidy. Because it looked like it was done right. And if I'd known one number — **3000W ÷ 12V = 250 amps** — and one question — **"where's the fuse relative to my battery?"** — I'd have asked. I wouldn't have needed to be an electrician to ask those two things.

That's what I want to get out of this post. Not that everyone's builder is bad. That you can ask better questions, and that the questions are simple.

**If you're waiting on a deposit right now, please read the Tasha section twice and get it in writing.** That's all I'd ask.

I'll post again when the van's back — what the rewire actually looked like, whether the batteries survived, whether insurance comes through, and whether I get Moose back on the road. In the meantime, if you're in the Halifax area and need a groomer, I've got a list of people I've referred to who are working and they're good. Drop a comment or DM me and I'll point you at them.

Talk soon. Take care of your vans, and please, **get a real electrician to look at your electrical.**

---

*One more thing for Tasha specifically, since I know you're the one reading this at 11pm: the $40 infrared thermometer is worth it before the van even arrives. I've got one I can lend you if you want to see what a normal reading looks like on a healthy setup — ask me and I'll dig it out. And seriously, email Darren the list. You don't have to be weird about it. "Before I pay the deposit, can you confirm the cable size and fuse specs in writing?" is a completely normal thing to say and it should be an easy yes.*

reasons: The piece says the dryer overloaded the cable 'every appointment, for five months', but the van was built in spring 2025 and the fire was Oct 28, 2026, which is far longer. It also invents details such as the narrator using her thermometer on Priya's van and Moose's mom becoming a regular.
